incremental.question: How does Verbatra avoid re-translating everything on every run?
incremental.answer: It keeps a committed lock file that records what was already translated. Each run diffs your source locale against that lock and sends only the new or changed keys to your provider. Unchanged keys are never touched, so a typical run costs a handful of strings, not your whole catalog.

providers.question: Which translation providers can I use?
providers.answer: Any of these, behind one interface: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Gemini (LLMs), DeepL and Google Cloud Translation (machine translation), openai-compatible, which points Verbatra at a local or self-hosted server like Ollama, LM Studio, or vLLM, and libretranslate, a self-hosted LibreTranslate server for machine translation with no language model. You pick one by id in the provider block of your config and switch later by rewriting that block, since each provider takes its own options. Gemini has a real free tier, and a local model costs nothing per call. Or set the provider to none to switch machine translation off entirely.

formats.question: Which formats and frameworks does Verbatra support?
formats.answer: JSON for i18next, vue-i18n, next-intl, and ngx-translate, plus XLIFF, YAML, Flutter ARB, Java/Spring .properties, Apple .strings and Xcode String Catalogs, Android strings.xml, gettext .po/.pot files, INI, and .NET .resx. That covers React, Next.js, Vue, Nuxt, Angular, SvelteKit, Astro, Node.js, Spring, Flutter, iOS, macOS, Android, and any gettext-based stack. Verbatra reads the files you already have; there is no Verbatra-specific format to migrate to.

ci.question: Can I run Verbatra in CI?
ci.answer: Yes. verbatra check calls no provider and exits 1 while a locale has missing or stale keys, so it gates a pull request without an API key. The GitHub Action runs check, diff or translate and reports the result as annotations and a job summary.

keys.question: Where do my API keys go?
keys.answer: Into environment variables, never into the config. The config rejects keys it does not know, so a secret cannot end up there by mistake. The CLI loads .env.local and .env for you, and an error names the missing variable but never prints a key.

privacy.question: Does Verbatra send my strings anywhere?
privacy.answer: Only to the translation provider you configure, and only when a command translates. Verbatra has no telemetry, analytics, or update check. You can switch machine translation off entirely, or run a model on your own hardware so nothing leaves your network. The <dataHandling>data handling page</dataHandling> lists what each provider receives and links each vendor's retention terms.

cost.question: What does Verbatra cost?
cost.answer: Verbatra itself is free and open source under the <license>MIT license</license>. The only cost is your provider's usage, which you control: it translates only what changed, and you can run it for free on Gemini's free tier or a local OpenAI-compatible model. Google's terms let it use free-tier requests to improve its products in some regions, so keep confidential strings on a paid tier or a local model; the <dataHandling>data handling page</dataHandling> links the current terms.

studio.question: Is Verbatra Studio a hosted service?
studio.answer: No. You start it in your project with verbatra studio, and it serves a dashboard on your machine. It calls no provider unless you start it with --allow-spend.

flow.heading: How the pieces connect.
flow.lead: One config file carries a change from your source locale through the CLI, CI and review to the coding agent in your editor.

source.title: Start from your source locale
source.body: Verbatra reads the locale files you already keep in your repository, in your framework's own format. The source locale stays the one file you edit by hand.

cli.title: Sync with the CLI
cli.body: `init` writes the config, and a dry run lists the keys a run would send without calling a provider. `translate` then fills every missing and changed key in each target locale.

incremental.title: Translate only what changed
incremental.body: The lock file stores a hash for every translated key, so a run skips what is done and sends only new or edited keys. The SDK runs the same incremental loop from your own script.
incremental.demo: Pick a change to a locale file below. Verbatra's own diff and hash code shows in your browser which keys a run would send, and translates nothing.

action.title: Translate in GitHub Actions
action.body: The action installs exactly the CLI version you pin and runs `translate` on every push to main, with your provider key from a repository secret. It never commits, so add your own step that commits the updated locale files, as the guide describes.

check.title: Fail a pull request on drift
check.body: `check` calls no provider and needs no key, so it can gate every pull request. It exits {fail} while a key is missing or stale, {ok} once every locale is in sync and {usage} on a usage or config error.

studio.title: Review in Verbatra Studio
studio.body: A local dashboard over your project. It shows where each locale stands and lets you fix a translation in place.

mcp.title: Hand it to your coding agent
mcp.body: Add this block to `.mcp.json`, and Claude Code starts the Verbatra MCP server over stdio. Your agent can then check translation status, use the glossary and correct a translation in place.

problem.heading: Locale files drift every time you ship.
problem.lead: Each feature adds strings, and someone has to find the keys every locale is missing. Pasting translations back by hand is where placeholders break.

missing.title: Missing keys reach production
missing.body: Nothing fails when the German file lacks a key. Users see the fallback language or the raw key.

wholeFile.title: Retranslating everything costs more
wholeFile.body: Sending the whole file again pays for strings that did not change and can replace wording someone fixed by hand.

placeholders.title: One broken placeholder breaks a screen
placeholders.body: A translation that drops a variable or garbles ICU plural syntax shows the wrong text, or none.

check.title: Check
check.body: `verbatra check` compares the source, the targets and the lock file. It calls no provider and needs no key.

translate.title: Translate
translate.body: `verbatra translate` sends only missing and changed keys, and refuses any result with mismatched placeholders, broken inline markup or invalid ICU syntax.

ci.title: Gate in CI
ci.body: The GitHub Action runs `check` on each pull request and fails it while a locale is out of sync.

bento.heading: Fits the project you already have.
bento.lead: Change the provider in one block, keep your keys in the environment and call the same engine from TypeScript.

providers.title: Switch providers in one block
providers.body: An LLM, a machine translation service, or a model on your own hardware. Change the provider block and keep the rest.
providers.none: Or turn machine translation off by policy, so every translation comes from a person.

keys.title: Your keys stay yours
keys.body: API keys come from environment variables only, never from the config file. Strings go to the provider you configure and nowhere else. No telemetry.

claims.data: An LLM receives your strings as data, never as instructions.
claims.integrity: A reply that breaks a placeholder or an ICU message is withheld, not written.
claims.errors: A missing key fails with an error that names the variable, never a value.

formats.title: Works with your files
formats.body: The same key, written the way each stack expects it. Verbatra reads and writes the files you already have, and a format it does not ship takes an adapter you build on the SDK.

sdk.title: A typed SDK
sdk.body: `translate` resolves to a typed `RunSummary`: which locales succeeded, which partly failed or failed, and the tokens the run used.

frameworks.title: A quickstart for your framework
frameworks.body: Each one goes from install to a translated file in your framework's own format.

code.heading: Use it from the terminal or from your own code.
code.lead: The CLI is built on the SDK, and the GitHub Action runs the CLI. Each reads the same config file.

captions.cli: Install, set up, preview without a key, translate, check.
captions.sdk: Translate and gate from your own script. The SDK reads the same config file.
captions.config: One committed file with no secrets in it. The API key comes from the environment.
captions.action: Fail a pull request while a locale is out of sync. No API key needed.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.languageVersions: This privacy policy is available in English, German, Spanish, and French. All four language versions have the same content and are equally binding.

s1.heading: 1. Responsible party
s1.body: The party responsible for data processing on this site is Mario Kreitz, Mönchfeldstraße 7, 70378 Stuttgart, Germany (the same details as in the <imprint>legal notice (Impressum)</imprint>). You can reach us by email at <email>info@kreitz-webdev.de</email>. No data protection officer has been appointed, because neither Art. 37 GDPR nor § 38 BDSG (German Federal Data Protection Act) requires one for this site.

s2.heading: 2. Overview
s2.body: This site is built to respect your privacy. It loads no third-party or analytics scripts in your browser, runs no cross-site tracking, sets a cookie only if you object to analytics (section 5), and collects only the minimal data needed to operate the site and understand aggregate usage. The sections below explain exactly what is processed and why.

s3.heading: 3. Server logs and hosting
s3.body: The site is self-hosted on a virtual server rented from <contabo>Contabo</contabo> (Contabo GmbH, Welfenstraße 22, 81541 Munich, Germany) and managed with Plesk. Contabo provides the server infrastructure and, in doing so, processes the data described in this section and in section 4 on our behalf as a processor (Art. 28 GDPR). When you visit, the web server processes standard access logs that may include your IP address, the date and time of the request, the requested URL, the referring page, and your browser's user-agent string. The application that serves the site also writes operational and error messages to its own container log, for example when a contact form notification cannot be sent. This data is used to operate and secure the site, for example to deliver pages, diagnose errors, and defend against abuse. The legal basis is Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (our legitimate interest in a secure, functioning service). The web server's access logs are deleted as soon as they are no longer needed for these purposes. The container log is rotated automatically and limited to 3 files of 10 MB each; once that limit is reached, the oldest file is deleted.

s4.heading: 4. Analytics
s4.body: We count page views with Umami, an open-source analytics tool that we host ourselves on the same server as this site (see section 3), so no analytics data is passed to a third party. No analytics script runs in your browser, and nothing is written to your device for counting page views. The only thing read from your device in connection with analytics is the opt-out cookie described in section 5, and only to honour your objection. Instead, when your browser loads a page of this site directly (not when it prefetches one in the background), our web server forwards the following details of that request to our Umami server: your IP address, your browser's user-agent string, the first language tag of your browser's Accept-Language header (for example en-US), which is forwarded with each page view, the referring page (without its query string) and the path of the page you loaded together with the five UTM parameters of the page address (utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term and utm_content, each shortened to 255 characters); all other query parameters, such as advertising click identifiers, and the fragment are discarded and not forwarded. Clicks, copied text and other interactions are not recorded. Your IP address and user-agent string themselves are not stored. The Umami server computes a pseudonymous session identifier by hashing the website ID, your IP address, your user-agent string, a value that changes every month and a secret key of the server. With each page view it stores that identifier, the time, the page path with any of those UTM parameters and the referring page, and for the session that language tag, your browser, operating system and device type (derived from the user-agent string), and your country, region and city, which it looks up from your IP address in a GeoLite2 database on the same server without contacting any other service. Because the session identifier is derived from your IP address, this is pseudonymous rather than anonymous processing of personal data. We only look at the results in aggregate and do not try to identify individual visitors. Because nothing is stored on your device for counting page views and the opt-out cookie is read only to honour your objection, no consent under § 25 TDDDG (German Telecommunications Digital Services Data Protection Act) is required for it. The legal basis for the processing is Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (our legitimate interest in understanding how the site is used). The analytics records are stored in the Umami database on this server. If your browser sends a Global Privacy Control (GPC) or Do Not Track signal, nothing is forwarded. You can also object with the button below: it sets the cookie described in section 5, and while your browser sends that cookie, nothing is forwarded either. An opt-out saved in your browser's local storage under this site's earlier analytics setup is no longer read; if you opted out that way, please opt out again here. You can read more about Umami in its documentation.

optOut.statusOptedOut: Saved: you have opted out. Your page views are not counted while this browser keeps the cookie.
optOut.statusOptedIn: Saved: analytics is allowed again. Your page views are counted unless your browser sends a GPC or Do Not Track signal.
optOut.signals: If your browser sends a Global Privacy Control (GPC) or Do Not Track signal, your page views are not counted, whichever button you choose. The buttons work without JavaScript.

s5.heading: 5. Cookies
s5.body: This site sets a cookie only when you object to analytics with the button in section 4: the cookie verbatra_analytics_optout with the value 1, valid for one year, which only stores your objection so that our server stops forwarding your page views. It is set only at your request and is strictly necessary for that purpose, so it needs no consent (§ 25(2) no. 2 TDDDG). Allowing analytics again deletes it. No other cookies are set. Two choices you make are saved in your browser's storage. When you switch between the light and dark theme, your choice is saved in local storage under the key theme. When you pick a package manager (npm, pnpm, yarn or bun) on the tabs above an install command, your choice is saved under the key package-manager in both local storage and session storage, so that the other install commands show the same package manager. Neither entry is written before you make that choice; both stay in your browser, are never sent to our server or anyone else, and you can delete them at any time by clearing this site's data in your browser. Because nothing requiring consent is stored on your device, no cookie consent banner is required.

s6.heading: 6. Fonts and assets
s6.body: Fonts and images, including the contributor avatars on the home page, are self-hosted: they are served from this site's own server, so loading a page makes no request to Google Fonts, GitHub, or any other third party. The site embeds no status badges. No third-party scripts, images, or embeds load at runtime, and no analytics script runs in your browser. External sites such as GitHub or npm are only contacted when you follow a link to them.

s7.heading: 7. GitHub and npm
s7.body: The project's source code, issues, and discussions are hosted on <repo>GitHub</repo>, and its published packages are hosted on <npm>npm</npm>. If you choose to interact on either site (for example, by opening an issue, joining a discussion, or viewing a package), that provider processes your data as an independent controller: <ghprivacy>GitHub's privacy statement</ghprivacy> or <npmprivacy>npm's privacy policy</npmprivacy> applies.

s8.heading: 8. Your rights
s8.body: Under the GDPR you have the rights of access, rectification, erasure, restriction of processing, objection, and data portability (Art. 15–21 GDPR); the right to object is set out separately in section 9. You also have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (Art. 77 GDPR). The supervisory authority responsible for us is "Der Landesbeauftragte für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit Baden-Württemberg" (the State Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information of Baden-Württemberg), Heilbronner Straße 35, 70191 Stuttgart, Germany, <lfdi>www.baden-wuerttemberg.datenschutz.de</lfdi>. To exercise any of these rights, contact us using the details below.

objection.heading: 9. Right to object (Art. 21 GDPR)
objection.body: Where we process your personal data on the basis of Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interests), as described in sections 3, 4, and 12, you have the right to object to that processing at any time, on grounds relating to your particular situation. If you object, we will no longer process the personal data concerned unless we can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds for the processing that override your interests, rights, and freedoms, or the processing serves the establishment, exercise, or defence of legal claims. An informal message to info@kreitz-webdev.de is enough to object.

s9.heading: 10. Contact
s9.body: For any privacy-related questions or requests, email <email>info@kreitz-webdev.de</email>.

s10.heading: 11. Changes to this policy
s10.body: We may update this privacy policy as the site evolves or as legal requirements change. The date below reflects the most recent revision.

s11.heading: 12. Contact form
s11.body: When you use the <contact>contact form</contact>, we process the name, email address, and message you submit in order to respond to your inquiry. The notification email is sent directly through our own mail server, hosted in Germany; no third-party email provider is involved in delivering it, and delivering it involves no transfer of data outside the EU. Besides the hosting provider (see section 3), the only processor involved under Art. 28 GDPR is Arcjet (Arcjet Labs, Inc., San Francisco, USA), which processes the request's IP address and headers (not the message content) through its Cloud API to protect the form against bots and abuse. According to <arcjetprivacy>Arcjet's privacy documentation</arcjetprivacy>, Arcjet retains this request data for 30 days and retains aggregated data derived from it for longer. Arcjet is based in the United States and does not guarantee that requests are processed in the EU, so this data may be transferred to the United States, a third country (Art. 44 ff. GDPR). Arcjet is not certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, so the European Commission's adequacy decision for that framework does not cover this transfer; it is instead based on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (Art. 46(2)(c) GDPR). You can request a copy of these safeguards by emailing <email>info@kreitz-webdev.de</email>. The legal basis is Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (our legitimate interest in operating the form securely and responding to inquiries). Your submission and the resulting notification email are not stored anywhere beyond the operator's inbox. They are deleted once your inquiry has been fully handled.

s12.heading: 13. AI-assisted translation
s12.body: This project, verbatra, is an AI-assisted translation tool, and this documentation site uses it on itself. English is the source language. The interface text (navigation, buttons, and similar strings) is machine-translated into German, Spanish, and French by verbatra with Google's Gemini language model. The documentation pages are translated with AI as well, in a separate step outside that automated pipeline. Some texts, including parts of these legal pages, were written or corrected directly instead of being generated by that pipeline. Translations are checked on a best-effort basis: not every translated text is reviewed by a person before it is published, so a translation may contain errors. If you notice one, please tell us through the <contact>contact form</contact>. We provide this information voluntarily, for transparency.
